title: Semantic satiation
hook: Say a word enough times and it turns into a strange, meaningless sound.
peek: Repeat a word out loud thirty times, any word, and it starts to sound foreign, then like noise. Psychologists have a name for this, coined in a 1962 doctoral thesis at McGill University.
lede: Pick a word, say 'spoon', and repeat it aloud for half a minute. Somewhere along the way it stops feeling like a word. It becomes a strange noise your mouth is making, and you may briefly wonder if it is spelled right. The effect was described in 1907, and the name semantic satiation came from a 1962 thesis by Leon Jakobovits James at McGill.

bullets.text: One leading explanation is that the brain's response to a repeated word briefly fades, so its meaning feels weaker. Rest a few moments and the meaning comes back. The effect works with written words too, if you stare at one long enough.
The opposite of déjà vu: something familiar suddenly feels new. Researchers who had people write a word over and over until it looked wrong won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2023.

A grammatical English sentence made of one word repeated eight times. Reading it is a good way to bring on satiation and puzzlement at once. It uses the word as a city, an animal and a verb meaning to bully.
The psychologist Diana Deutsch found that a spoken phrase, looped many times, starts to sound sung. Like the Shepard tone, it shows repetition reshaping what we hear.
Two American psychologists had people stare at a printed word for minutes at a time. Many said it began to look strange and lose its meaning, the same effect seen rather than heard.
